extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (managers, planners, evaluators)
extracted.subtask_description: Planning, researching, executing, and evaluating public relations programs using the behavioral "molecule" (detect → construct → define → select → confirm → behave → detect) and developing measurable goals and objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral molecule as a management process
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers should use the behavioral molecule (detect → construct → define → select → confirm → behave → detect) to plan professional behaviors and public relations programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the full sequence to (1) detect problems, (2) construct alternatives, (3) define costs/methods, (4) select an alternative, (5) confirm risks/consequences, (6) behave (execute), and (7) detect (evaluate feedback). If a manager cannot choose an alternative, return to construct; if objectives are not met, return to construct and iterate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different information needs for each molecule segment
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers need different kinds of information in each segment of the behavioral molecule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect: information about existence of PR problems; Construct: research to understand the problem, identify publics, and review case studies; Define: information on costs, methods, and consequences of alternatives; Select: may seek information to form referent criteria but 'information has the least value'—manager must stop communicating and decide; Confirm: further information on consequences to validate earlier data; Behave: information to check program implementation and whether technicians need assistance; Second Detect: evaluative feedback from the environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of referent criteria in selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers may apply decision rules from previous experience (referent criteria) to eliminate alternatives and speed decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referent criteria function as rules of thumb; they can be prior successful methods, values or attitudes (e.g., rejecting press manipulation because it conflicts with professional values). Be aware that reliance on referent criteria can both save time and carry over inappropriate biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirm segment — risk analysis before behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: After selecting a behavior, managers should confirm that the selected behavior will work and is the best alternative by thinking through potential failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Murphy’s law: consider everything that could go wrong and the damage if it does. If risk is acceptable, proceed to behave; if risk is too great, return to construct or select for alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select segment — decision finality and communication limits
rubrics_metrics.description: In the select segment, the manager must stop communicating and make a decision; excessive information or communication here merely prolongs the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information has least value in the select segment; use referent criteria if helpful, but avoid delaying action by continual discussion or data-gathering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behave segment — execution responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The behave segment is where managers 'do something' (write a news story, hold an open house, contact leaders); communication technicians execute the program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan implementation tasks clearly and assign execution to technicians; ensure mechanisms exist to support technicians and monitor rollout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect (second) — evaluative feedback loop
rubrics_metrics.description: After behavior, managers must examine feedback to detect whether objectives have been met; success means continue, failure means return to construct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evaluative research and monitoring to determine outcomes and feed results back into the molecule to iterate or scale actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative vs evaluative research timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Formative research takes place before a program (first detect, construct, define, select, confirm); evaluative research takes place after a behavior (second detect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design research activities appropriate to timing: formative to plan and pretest, evaluative to measure outcomes and objectives after implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Environmental monitoring is research to detect trends in public opinion and in the social-political climate of the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use environmental monitoring during the detect segment to identify emerging issues and contextual trends that may require PR attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social auditing
rubrics_metrics.description: Social auditing determines the consequences the organization has had on its publics and the extent to which the organization must correct those consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat social audits as a detect-segment activity that assesses ethical/social impacts and obligations to publics; use findings to inform program design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations auditing
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations auditing is research to define publics and to determine how these publics perceive and evaluate the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations audits begin in the detect segment and provide much information for the construct segment: who relevant publics are, how the organization stands, which issues concern publics, and publics’ power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication auditing
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication auditing evaluates whether messages have actually got through to receivers (readership surveys, content analysis, readability measures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use communication audits as evaluative methods in define and confirm segments for pretesting messages and in the second detect segment to measure PR objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives must be specific and measurable
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectives are 'ends in view'—expected solutions to day-to-day problems that are specific and measurable, unlike broader goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write objectives in measurable terms (e.g., 'get 30% of Washington Post readers to understand the position' or 'write the ad clearly so readers comprehend it'). Objectives allow planning of activities and post-program evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think in terms of effect, not process
rubrics_metrics.description: PR planning and evaluation should focus on effects (what the project should accomplish) rather than only on processes or outputs (how many releases, when the report is done).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining a problem and objectives, ask what communication effect is necessary and whether it is reasonable and measurable; design activities that logically contribute to those effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish goals (broad) from objectives (specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Goals are generalized ends that provide a framework for decision making but are too broad for day-to-day decisions; objectives are specific steps that contribute to goals and are measurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top managers typically set goals (two-way communication, mutual understanding, public acceptance); middle managers and technicians set objectives that move the organization toward those goals and can be evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who decides goals vs objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Top PR managers (vice president/director) are responsible for choosing departmental goals; middle managers and practitioners are responsible for selecting program- and task-level objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand role distinctions: macro-decisions (goals, budgets, organizational alignment) vs micro-decisions (measurable objectives, tactics, day-to-day management).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use objectives to justify PR value to top management
rubrics_metrics.description: Because goals are broad and hard to measure, PR practitioners must demonstrate value to the organization by showing how measurable objectives contributed to organizational effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and present evaluation data (media use, readership, attitude measures) that link PR activities to organizational subsystems' performance to defend budgets and resource needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational effectiveness perspectives for PR evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational effectiveness can be judged by (1) attainment of organizational goals and (2) ability to survive/adapt and acquire resources from the environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize multiple definitions of effectiveness; PR contributions should be articulated in terms that matter to the organization—helping achieve goals or helping control/adapt to the environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication's dual role: control and adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication can be used to control (persuasion) or to adapt (understanding) other groups; PR helps the organization survive and adapt by employing both functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design PR objectives and tactics that either aim to influence publics (control) or to gather and respond to public needs (adaptation), depending on organizational strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid management mistakes by following the molecule
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems that include each segment of the behavioral molecule will adapt and survive; skipping segments or misordering them leads to common mistakes (dogmatism, habit, procrastination, indecision, perfectionism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rush to outputs (e.g., habitually banging out a release when criticized); ensure you go through detect/construct/define/select/confirm before behaving to reduce errors and improve outcomes.
